newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Kia union support seen reassuring jittery lenders.
newsitem.headline: Kia union support seen reassuring jittery lenders.

text.p: South Korea's beleaguered Kia Group received good news on Thursday when the labour union of its automaking arm agreed to let management set this year's wage increase, a move analysts said would reassure skittish lenders.
Kia Motors Corp said the union decision had opened a new chapter in the Kia Group's previously contentious labour-management relations and would help change attitudes towards the group.

"Management has fully explained about the company's financial position and asked for our understanding. To break the chain of financial pressures, we needed a tangible decision," union chairman Lee Seung-jae told reporters.

South Korea's eighth-largest conglomerate, the Kia Group has been battered by rumours of financial troubles for months, leaving lenders reluctant to extend credits, especially in the aftermath of a string of corporate collapses since early this year.
Analysts said the union's decision would help reassure both lenders and the government that the company's past labour disruptions would not be repeated this year.

"The government's attitude is an important factor when banks consider whether to give additional loans," said Sohn Jong-won, an analyst at Ssangyong Investment and Securities. "The union's decision will help change the government's attitude."
Investors welcomed the news and Kia Motors shares soared by its daily limit of 1,000 won ($1.13) to 14,600 won shortly after the announcement was made.
A peaceful relationship with Kia's labour union, regarded as one of the nation's most militant, would contribute to the company's earnings, analysts said.
"The decision will contribute to improving productivity and beef up Kia's corporate image among consumers and other people," said Lee Hahn-koo, president of the Daewoo Research Institute.
Kia Group chairman Kim Sun-hong recently asked finance minister Kang Kyong-shik to persuade merchant banks to keep cash flowing to the conglomerate.
Kia Group officials were meeting with merchant bankers on Thursday to persuade them to keep credit lines open.
The group has presented a plan to restructure and tide over what group officials described as temporary cash-flow problems.
Asia Motors, the group's commercial vehicle arm, said it would raise about 520 billion won by moving its plant to a cheaper site two to three years ahead of schedule.
The group also said it would sell some 795 billion won worth of idle assets.

Kia's difficulties were exacerbated after an internal report by rival Samsung Motors Inc was leaked. It suggested the nation's crowded car industry be restructured to survive and hinted at a possible takeover bid.

Kia Motors has been viewed as a takeover target because of its thinly spread shareholdings. Kia's largest shareholder Ford Motor Co holds 16.91 percent, with no management rights. Kia employees hold 13.81 percent.
Kia Motors' total debts were estimated at 5.6 trillion won at the end of 1996, against net worth of 1.3 trillion won and total assets of 2.68 trillion won.
